## Precision Genome Editing Strategies to Treat Sickle Cell Disease and

## CDKL5 Deficiency Disorder

## Abstract

There are over 70,000 known mutations that cause genetic disease. Genome editing

technologies could enable the life-long correction of such pathogenic mutations, potentially

improving the lives of thousands of rare disease patients worldwide. Nuclease-based genome

editing tools lead to double strand breaks which result in stochastic indel formation. Therefore,

these tools lack the precision to exactly correct many pathogenic mutations. Furthermore,

nuclease-based editing can lead to undesired consequences such as p53 activation, large

deletions, and chromothripsis among other unwanted outcomes. Development of genome

editing strategies that can precisely correct pathogenic mutations and do not rely on double

strand break formation could be transformative for the study and therapeutic landscape of

genetic disorders. My doctoral studies have focused on developing clinically relevant precision

genome editing strategies for two rare diseases: sickle cell disease (SCD), a devastating

inherited blood disorder, and for CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD), a catastrophic early-onset

pediatric seizure disorder.

First, I describe the development of a clinically relevant base editing strategy for SCD.

While adenine base editors (ABEs) cannot directly correct the pathogenic A•T-to-T•A mutation

that causes the disease, base editors can convert the pathogenic sickle allele (HBBS) into a


<!-- Page 7 -->


iv

benign and naturally-occurring Makassar allele (HBBG). We utilized ABE8e-NRCH, a bespoke

ABE with both an evolved SpCas9 nickase and an evolved adenine deaminase domain. With ex

vivo electroporation of ABE8e-NRCH mRNA and a synthetic single guide RNA (sgRNA) into

hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) from sickle cell disease patients, we were

able to achieve up to 80% conversion of HBBS to HBBG. We transplanted these edited cells into

irradiated mice and found that sixteen weeks post-transplantation, Makassar β-globin comprised

79% of all β-globins in the blood, and that hypoxic sickling was significantly reduced.

Additionally, mice that were transplanted with ABE8e-NRCH base-edited murine HSPCs had a

statically significant reduction in hallmark sickle cell pathology. Furthermore, secondary

transplantation of treated HSPCs revealed HBBS-to-HBBG correction was durable in long-term,

bone marrow-repopulating hematopoietic stem cells. Compared to Cas9 nuclease treatment,

base edited HSPCs avoided large deletions and activation of the p53-mediated DNA damage

response. Our study demonstrated that ex vivo base editing represents one clinically relevant

precision genome editing strategy that could be curative for SCD.

Second, I describe the development of a clinically relevant prime editing strategy to

directly revert the sickle cell allele back to wild-type hemoglobin. We used prime editing tools

with improved architectures, namely PEmax and an engineered pegRNA (epegRNA). With ex

vivo electroporation of PEmax mRNA and synthetic nicking sgRNAs, we were able to achieve

up to 41% correction in HSPCs from sickle cell patients. Seventeen weeks after transplantation

into immunodeficient mice, the prime-edited patient HSPCs retained HBBS-to-HBBA conversion

and lineage potential. In addition, 28-43% of β-globins expressed in human reticulocytes

isolated post-transplantation were wild-type adult hemoglobin, proportional to initial levels of

editing. Edited cells also had a statically significant reduction in hypoxic sickling. Our

experimentally unbiased off-target editing analysis at over 100 sites revealed minimal off-target

editing. Compared to strategies that utilize Cas9 nuclease-mediated homology directed repair

(HDR) to correct HBBS, our prime editing strategy has unique advantages like not requiring DSB


<!-- Page 8 -->


v

formation or the delivery of an exogenous donor DNA template. Our study provides evidence

that one-time ex vivo prime editing of patient HSPCs is a viable and clinically relevant precision

genome editing strategy for the correction of the sickle cell allele.

Finally, I describe the development of a prime editing strategy to correct various

mutations causing CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD). We used evolved prime editors (PE6

variants) to screen correction strategies for two causative CDD mutations in patients,

c.1412delA and c.826-1 G > A. For c.1412delA, we developed and tested corrective prime

editing strategies in several preclinical models—both a murine and a human cell line with the

pathogenic mutation, and primary patient fibroblasts, with future studies planned for the relevant

mouse model and cortical organoids differentiated from patient-derived iPSCs. Using an

evolved SpCas9 (SpCas9-NRCH) DNA-targeting domain, we can target the disease allele in a

murine cell line and achieve 38% correction with PE6b-NRCH and PE6c-NRCH. In a

homozygous c.1412delA-containting HEK293T line, we achieved to 33% and 30% correction of

the pathogenic using PE6c and PE6d respectively. PE6c editing in primary fibroblasts from the

patient with the c.1412delA mutation reached 28% correction with a high degree of DNA

specificity. Furthermore, we observed up to 9% correction for the c.826-1 G > A mutation with

PE6c in initial prime editing screens, and nearly 30% installation of replacement of a hotspot

region of exon 8 that harbors a variety of CDKL5 pathogenic mutations. Our studies

demonstrate the potential use of prime editing to correct multiple causative CDD mutations.

## Chapter 1 : Introduction

### 1.1 Introduction to therapeutic genome editing

1.1.1 Human genetic disease and genome editing tools

Approximately 3 billion base pairs encode the human genome, but even a single

mutation amongst those base pairs can lead to genetic disease. Currently, there are over

75,000 known pathogenic mutations which are caused by single base mutations, small

deletions, duplications, copy number loss, and other genetic changes1 (Figure 1.1). Gene

therapy is best suited for patients with mutations that cause loss of gene function or

haploinsufficiency as it can deliver a functional copy of the missing or ineffectively expressed

gene. In contrast, genome editing can address a variety of pathogenic mutations regardless of

how they manifest through direct and permanent correction of pathogenic mutations without

requiring persistent expression of the genome editor and while keeping the target gene under

endogenous transcriptional control.

Genome editing technologies are revolutionizing how genetic disorders are treated. The

FDA has recently approved its first CRISPR-based genome editing therapeutic for sickle cell

disease2, a catastrophic inherited blood disorder. While this transformative and potentially

curative therapeutic option is an important step forward in the development and approval of

genome editing therapies, it utilizes a nuclease-based strategy with inherent limitations around

uncontrollable insertion and deletion (indel) byproducts, precision, and genotoxicities. Thus, the

development of precision genome editing strategies with minimal indel formation, reduced off-

target editing (or editing at sites beyond the intended locus), and fewer genotoxicities is

imperative in order to offer patients potentially curative therapeutics that are as robust, safe, and

effective as possible.

1.1.2 CRISPR/Cas9 nuclease editing

The bacterial adaptive immune system integrates short repeat fragments of DNA from

pathogenic bacteriophage into the host bacteria genome. These unique spacer sequences are a

component of clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR) loci. Once

transcribed, these CRISPR loci are processed into CRISPR-derived RNAs (crRNAs) and

packaged into a surveillance complex with CRISPR-associated (Cas) proteins to seek and

destroy complementary foreign nucleic acids, much like an eukaryotic RNA interference (RNAi)

mechanism4. Researchers have utilized CRISPR and its associated proteins and RNAs to

catalyze genome editing in mammalian cells5,6.

A variety of CRISPR systems and their associated proteins have been discovered7–9,

though the most commonly used for genome editing is SpCas9 from Streptococcus pyrgenes10.

The crRNA and trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) for SpCas9 can be fused into a single guide

RNA (sgRNA)10. When the sgRNA is bound to the SpCas9 ribonucleoprotein, the entire

ribonucleoprotein complex can be targeted to a genomic locus of interest through simple

reprogramming of the protospacer sequence to any other protospacer sequence, given it is


<!-- Page 18 -->


3

immediately proceeded by an appropriate protospacer adjacent motif (PAM), the sequence

requirements of which varies for each Cas protein11.

After the SpCas9 protein is localized via the sgRNA to the target locus with an

appropriate NGG PAM, it creates a double-strand break (DSB) three nucleotides upstream of

the PAM through cleavage of the phosphodiester backbone of both DNA strands12. DSBs can

be repaired by the cell through competing mechanisms, namely non-homologous end joining

(NHEJ)13,14 or homology directed repair (HDR)15. NHEJ and a related process called

microhomology-mediated repair (MMEJ)16,17 are error-prone repair mechanisms, resulting

uncontrollable, but predictable insertion and deletions (indels) at DSBs in the target sequence18

(Figure 1.2). These error-prone repair mechanisms are often utilized to knock-out genes and

subsequent protein activity, or to disrupt binding sites for enhancers, activators, or repressors.

FDA-approved Casgevy relies on Cas9 nuclease-mediated disruption of the BCL11A erythroid-

specific enhancer locus to reactive fetal hemoglobin as a treatment for sickle cell disease2, but

this strategy can stimulate DNA damage responses or lead to BCL11A allele loss in the

therapeutic cell type, hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs)19. Another example of

Cas9 nuclease-mediated disruption would be reactivation of fetal hemoglobin expression

through disruption of the BLC11A repressor binding site in the γ-globin (HBG) promoter20,21.

However, various indel-containing alleles at both the HBG promoter and the BCL11A erythroid-

specific enhancer locus have been demonstrated to have different phenotypic outcomes22,

which can lead to variable therapeutic response in HSPCs, and ultimately in patients.

If a homologous DNA donor is provided, cells may repair DSBs using the DNA donor as

a template to incorporate the desired edits15 (Figure 1.2). HDR is inefficient in non-dividing cells,

limiting its therapeutic utility in post-mitotic cell types23,24. Homology-independent targeted

integration (HITI) is an alternative to HDR that can be achieved in non-diving cells, though it still

relies on delivery of a donor template and additionally on NHEJ25. While the desired edit can be

incorporated via nuclease-mediated HDR or HITI, indel outcomes often exceed perfect desired

Once Cas9 nuclease binds and cleaves its target site, the presence or absence of a DNA donor will determine how the DSB is repaired by the cell.

and other unintended chromosomal abnormalities37–43. And while engineered higher fidelity

Cas9 variants can reduce undesired off-target editing44–51, these variants generally have

lowered on-target editing efficiencies, nor do they support alternative methods of reducing off-

targets such as sgRNA engineering52. Thus, efficient and precise correction of pathogenic

1.1.3 Precision genome editing with base editors

To address some limitations inherent to Cas9 nuclease editing, our group developed

base editors53,54. Base editors are comprised of a catalytically impaired Cas9 nickase tethered

to either a cytosine deaminase (cytosine base editor or CBE53, Figure 1.3a), or a an evolved

adenine deaminase (adenine base editor or ABE55, Figure 1.3b). Base editors are localized to

the target DNA locus via an sgRNA. After localization, the Cas9 nickase unwinds the DNA,

creating an R-loop, or a stretch of single-stranded DNA that the deaminases can use as a

substrate. CBEs deaminate cytosine into uridine, which is read as thymine by DNA

polymerases. ABEs follow a similar process, deaminating adenine into inosine which is read as

guanine by DNA polymerases. Opposite strand nicking helps to bias DNA repair outcomes

toward the desired edit53. The addition of two uracil glycosylase inhibitors on the CBE

additionally encourage desired DNA outcomes by inhibiting native uracil glycosylase which

attempt to resolve the strand by excising the generated uracil intermediate53.

The deaminase domains of base editors have also undergone directed evolution or

engineering efforts, resulting in base editors that are faster and more processive65 or that can

perform novel deamination functions with low off-target activity66,67 among other desirable

characteristics. Various studies have focused on the creation and use of minimized base

editors61,65,66,68, which is particularly relevant for therapeutic applications. Adeno-associated

viruses (AAVs) are an FDA-approved delivery method for in vivo gene therapy and gene editing

therapeutics69. The packaging limit for AAVs is around 4.7kb excluding the inverted terminal

repeats70,71, a limit that is generally too small to efficiently package base editors and other

necessary components for efficient editing including the sgRNA, promoters, and cis-regulatory

elements. Our group has previously shown that base editors can be delivered in vivo with a dual

AAV strategy72 and we have recently developed a highly-efficient, single AAV delivery strategy

for ABE using size-minimized components and an ABE8e deaminase73. Use of a single AAV

simplifies the delivery and manufacture of a potential base editing therapeutic, in addition to

minimizing the required dose of AAV, important steps for the therapeutic application of base

editors.

Base editors have already entered clinical trials74, most notably with a PSCK9-targeting

ABE that disrupts PSCK9 function to lower low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) in

patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia75. In another clinical trial, healthy

donor T cells were edited ex vivo with a codon-optimized CBE targeting TRBC1 and TRBC2,

CD7, and CD52 to create base-edited CAR7 (BE-CAR7) T cells for the treatment of highly

aggressive T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia76. Yet another base editor clinical trial has

recently dosed its first sickle cell disease patients with an ABE therapy aimed at reactivating

fetal hemoglobin expression77,78. The work detailed in this dissertation covers an alternative

base editing approach to treat sickle cell disease through the conversion of the sickle cell allele

(HBBS) to the naturally occurring, non-pathogenic Makassar allele (HBBG)19. I also describe the

use of prime editing to directly revert the sickle cell allele back to the wild type allele (HBBA)79.

Base editing offers many advantages over Cas9 nuclease genome editing. First, base

editing does not require double strand breaks (DSBs), consequently generating fewer undesired

byproducts such as uncontrolled mixtures of indel alleles, large deletions42, chromosomal loss38,

chromothripsis37, and p53 activation40,41 among other unwanted outcomes. Cas9-meidated

homology directed repair can be difficult to achieve in some quiescent cells types, whereas

base editing is still efficient in non-dividing cells80. Furthermore, Cas9 nuclease editing results in

a variety of allele outcomes, and the phenotypic consequences of each of these indel-containing

alleles may not correlate with the desired outcome22. In contrast, base editing results in a high

desired edit-to-indel ratio, leading to fewer indel alleles and more predictable phenotypic

outcomes22.  While precise, base editors can exhibit minimal levels of off-target DNA or RNA

editing. Many base editor variants have been described that reduce off-target editing without

sacrificing on-target activity55,65,68,81–84.

While base editors offer many advantages, there are limitations to their use as well.

Base editors can only perform transition mutations, that is C-to-T edits or vice versa, and A-to-G

edits or vice versa. Though transition mutations account for 30% of all known pathogenic alleles

(Figure 1.1), base editing cannot correct the transversion, deletion, insertion, or duplication

mutations that make up the other 70% of known pathogenic variants. Fortunately, prime editing

can correct >99% of known pathogenic alleles while retaining some of the advantages of base

editors3.

1.1.4 Precision genome editing with prime editors

Prime editors are comprised of a Cas9 nickase tethered to an engineered Moloney

murine leukemia virus (M-MLV) reverse transcriptase (RT), and they can enable all base-to-

base pair changes, including transversion mutations, in addition to insertions, deletions, or any

combination thereof3. Prime editors are localized to the target DNA site by a prime editing guide

RNA (pegRNA)3. PegRNAs are similar to sgRNAs but also include a 3’ extension with a primer

template (RTT), which the RT uses as a substrate. After PBS priming, the reverse transcriptase

of the prime editor then polymerizes the desired edits from the RTT directly into the DNA3. A

nicking sgRNA may also be included to nick the opposite strand and bias DNA repair outcomes

toward the desired edit (PE3, Figure 1.4).

Prime editors can install transition and transversion point mutations, small insertions, small deletions, or any combination thereof with high levels of desired editing and minimal indel formation.

and PACE. One engineering strategy to improve prime editing outcomes is the addition of a

dominant negative form of MLH1 (MLH1dn)86, a protein implicated in mismatch repair (MMR).

Single base pair mismatches between newly synthesized and endogenous DNA can be

recognized as an MMR signal. Inhibition of MMR leads to improved prime editing outcomes86,87,

and can be achieved through MLH1dn co-delivery both with (PE5, Figure 1.4) or without (PE4,

Other improvements to prime editors which are particularly helpful for their therapeutic

application include PEmax86, the PE6 variants88, and engineered pegRNAs (epegRNAs)89.

PEmax improves the original PE2 architecture through extensive Cas9 and nuclear localization

sequence (NLS) optimization and optimized codon usage86. PEmax unilaterally improves prime

editing outcomes in cell lines, primary cells, and patient-derived cells compared to the original

PE2 architecture79,86.

The PE6 (PE6a-PE6g) variants were developed through a combination of PACE and

protein engineering to generate size-minimized editors with improved efficiency88. Size-

minimized prime editors are particularly relevant in considerations of viral delivery. AAV is an

FDA-approved viral delivery method for gene therapies69,90. However, the 4.7kb packaging limit

of AAV is greatly exceeded by the size of the full-length prime editor and all essential editing

components, requiring a triple AAV delivery strategy for efficient editing unless the RNase-H

domain of the RT is removed91. PE6 editors are sufficiently compact enough for dual AAV

delivery while retaining or exceeding PEmax efficiencies, both in vitro in patient-derived and

primary cells, and in vivo in the murine brain88. As with base editors, minimizing the number of

AAVs required for in vivo prime editing simplifies delivery, manufacture, and dose requirements

which are important considerations for therapeutic development.

Engineered pegRNAs (epegRNAs) include a structured 3’ motif which improves pegRNA

stability in cells and protects the pegRNA from degradation from endogenous exonucleases89.

One important detail to consider in the development of epegRNAs was the compatibility

between the structured 3’ motif and chemical modifications such as 2′-O-methyl and

phosphorothioate linkages that are commonly used in synthetic guide RNA formulation to

increase resistance to exonucleolytic degradation92,93. We were able to show that epegRNAs

Though prime editors have not yet entered the clinic, they have enabled robust

corrective editing in model systems for many diseases like sickle cell disease79, CDKL5

deficiency disorder, and many other diseases across various tissues like the liver, eye, and

vivo HSPC editing for chronic granulomatous disease95,96. Future clinical trials for prime editing

may also be pursued for Wilson’s disease, retinitis pigmentosa, and Friedreich’s ataxia95,96.

Prime editors also offer many advantages over Cas9 nuclease-mediated genome

editing. Like base editing, prime editing does not require DSB formation, which reduces indel

formation and avoids common outcomes of DSBs like chromosomal abnormalities as previously

discussed. Many studies have reported that off-target editing with prime editors is minimal79 and

substantially lower in comparison to other genome editing tools97–105. Additionally, prime editing

Prime editors and base editors are complementary tools in genome editing. Base editors

can only perform transition mutations while prime editors can encode all base-to-base changes.

Even though prime editors can make the same types of changes as base editors, base editing

outperforms prime editing when the target adenine or cytosine is well-positioned in the editing

window3. However, bystander editing, or editing of other adenines or cytosines beyond the

target base in the editing window, can be avoided by using a prime editor. In this work, I discuss

both a base19 and a prime79 editing strategy for corrective editing of the sickle cell allele,

highlighting the utility of both precision genome editing tools. Given their uniquely prime-editable

nature, I also I discuss several prime editing strategies for pathogenic variants in the CDKL5

gene which cause CDKL5 deficiency disorder. Practical application of base and prime editors to

sickle cell disease and CDKL5 deficiency disorder represent an important step toward the

development of precision genome editing therapeutics for rare diseases.

### 2.1 Introduction

Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutation of HBB, which

normally encodes adult β-globin (βA) (Figure 2.1a). At low oxygen concentrations, the mutant β-

globin (βS) causes hemoglobin polymerization within red blood cells (RBCs), which results in

characteristic sickle-shaped RBCs and a cascade of hemolysis, inflammation, and

microvascular occlusions. Symptoms include anemia, severe acute and chronic pain,

immunodeficiency, multi-organ failure and early death106. Although allogeneic hematopoietic

stem cell (HSC) transplantation can cure SCD, optimally matched donors are usually not

available and the procedure can result in graft rejection or graft-versus-host disease107–110.

Ex vivo modification of autologous HSCs to circumvent the deleterious effects of the

SCD mutation underlies several experimental therapies111–115. Approaches that have shown

early clinical promise include ectopic expression of an anti-sickling β-like globin gene by

lentiviral vectors116 and induction of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) by suppression117 or Cas9-mediated

disruption118 of BCL11A. Lentiviral vectors carry risks of insertional mutagenesis, however, and

may not effectively suppress the expression of pathological βS. Genetic manipulation to induce

expression of HbF does not eliminate βS, and when mediated by double-stranded DNA breaks

(DSBs), carries risks associated with uncontrolled mixtures of indels (insertions and deletion),

translocations, loss of large chromosomal segments, chromothripsis, and p53 activation18,37,38,40–

43,119–121. Cas9 nuclease-mediated homology-directed repair can correct HBBS but is difficult to

achieve efficiently in repopulating HSCs26,122 and also requires DSBs. Elimination of the root

cause of SCD by converting the HBBS allele to a benign variant without introducing DSBs could

overcome these limitations.

Adenine base editors (ABEs) convert targeted A•T base pairs to G•C in living cells

without requiring DSBs or donor DNA templates, and with minimal formation of indels65. In SCD,

the GAG (Glu) codon that encodes amino acid 6 of β-globin is mutated to GTG (Val). Although

adenine base editing cannot revert this mutation, it can convert the pathogenic codon to GCG


<!-- Page 30 -->


15

(Ala), which produces a naturally occurring, non-pathogenic variant termed Hb-Makassar

(HBBG)60,123–126 (Figure 2.1a).

We generated an ABE (ABE8e-NRCH60,65) that converts the SCD allele to the non-

pathogenic HBBG Makassar allele with minimal non-silent bystander edits in CD34+ HSPCs from

patients with SCD. Edited HSPCs were durable after engraftment in mice, with an HBBG

frequency of 68% sixteen weeks after transplantation and markedly reduced sickling in the

derived erythroid cells. To assess phenotypic rescue, we edited HSPCs from a mouse model of

SCD127 in which endogenous β-globin genes are replaced by human HBBS, and transplanted

the edited HSPCs into irradiated adult recipient mice. Primary and secondary transplantation of

edited mouse HSPCs confirmed editing in long-term HSCs and restored hematological

parameters to near-normal levels. These findings show that autologous ex vivo base editing and

transplantation of HSCs is a potential one-time treatment for SCD.

### 2.2 Results

2.2.1 HBBS base editing in HSPCs

The HBBS mutation can be targeted by base editing using a phage-assisted continuous

evolution (PACE)-generated Cas9-NRCH60 that recognizes a CACC protospacer-adjacent motif

(PAM; Figure 2.1a). Separately, we used PACE to evolve TadA-8e, a deoxyadenosine

deaminase that supports highly efficient base editing65. We combined TadA-8e with Cas9-

NRCH nickase to generate ABE8e-NRCH. Co-delivery of ABE8e-NRCH and the HBBS -

targeting single guide RNA (sgRNA) to homozygous HBBS HEK293T cells by plasmid

lipofection achieved 58% conversion of HBBS to HBBG.

Next, we used ABE8e-NRCH to edit human HSPCs ex vivo through electroporation of

either the ABE8e-NRCH + sgRNA ribonucleoprotein (RNP) or ABE8e-NRCH mRNA with

sgRNA. ABE8e-NRCH RNP electroporated into plerixafor-mobilized peripheral blood CD34+

HSPCs cells from three donors with SCD resulted in 44 ± 5.9% (mean ± s.d.) editing of HBBS to


<!-- Page 31 -->

HBBG, 1.2 ± 0.33% indels, and less than 0.5% other missense alleles after 6 days.

Electroporation of ABE8e-NRCH mRNA and sgRNA into the same cells resulted in 80 ± 2.1%

conversion of HBBS to HBBG, 2.8 ± 0.50% indels, and less than 2% other missense bystander

alleles (Figure 2.1b). Thus, introduction of ABE8e-NRCH RNP or mRNA using a clinically

relevant delivery method can convert HBBS to HBBG in HSPCs efficiently and with few

byproducts.

HSPCs from patients with SCD (referred to as SCD cells) that had been edited with

ABE8e-NRCH mRNA or RNP were differentiated ex vivo into late-stage erythroid precursors.

Quantification of β-like globin proteins by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)

showed that unedited SCD cells contained 87 ± 1.3% βS and no detectable βG, whereas base-

edited cells contained 72 ± 3.0% βG and 17 ± 3.0% βS, a 5.1-fold decrease in the pathogenic βS

protein (Figure 2.1c). These findings show that ABE8e-NRCH-mediated editing of HBBS results

in substantial production of βG and concomitant loss of βS protein.

To assess the effects of editing on sickling, we incubated purified reticulocytes from ex

vivo differentiation of unedited or ABE8e-NRCH-edited SCD CD34+ cells in 2% oxygen. Editing

reduced sickling frequency from 47.7% to 16.3% (Figure 2.1d, e), confirming that HBBS-to-HBBG

conversion reduced sickling. Reticulocytes that were differentiated from cells treated with

ABE8e-NRCH RNP showed similar results, but with lower efficiencies (Figure 2.1 c–e).

To determine whether base editing alters erythropoiesis, we used flow cytometry to track

the expression of the cell-surface maturation markers CD49d, CD235a and BAND3. We found

no differences in the expression of these markers between edited and unedited cells,

suggesting that editing with ABE8e-NRCH does not alter erythropoiesis.

### 2.3 Discussion

We describe a bespoke ABE that directly converts the major SCD allele to a β-globin

variant that is non-pathogenic, even in homozygous123 or hemizygous125 form. This base editing

strategy was efficient (up to 80% editing in HSPCs and 68% in bone marrow-repopulating

HSCs), with minimal bystander edits or indels, and yielded non-sickling RBCs without disruption

of globin gene regulation or hematopoiesis.

Several approaches for autologous therapies to treat SCD are being tested in clinical

trials111,112,116–118. It is not yet known which strategy is safest or most effective. However, the

base editing approach demonstrated here offers several potential advantages. First, elimination

of the disease-causing mutation by precise HBBS-to-HBBG editing may reduce the concentration

of sickle hemoglobin in RBCs (the primary determinant of pathogenic hemoglobin

polymerization) more effectively than lentiviral expression of β-like globin or induction of HbF,

both of which leave HBBS alleles intact. Although the latter approaches can decrease the

fraction of βS in erythroid progeny by 30–70%135,136, we achieved even greater βS reduction in

erythroid populations by base editing HBBS.

Second, base editing largely avoids DSBs generated by nucleases, which lead to

uncontrolled mixtures of indels at the target site as well as large deletions, translocations,

chromosomal loss, chromothripsis, and activation of the p53 DNA damage response18,37,38,40–

43,119–121. Treatment of HSPCs with ABE8e-NRCH did not lead to a detected p53 response or

large deletions, in contrast to treatment with Cas9 nuclease (Figure 2.5).

Third, base editing does not require DNA delivery, which is a requirement for gene

therapy or homology-directed repair. The introduction of DNA can lead to toxicity and insertional

mutagenesis114,137,138. By contrast, base editing using mRNA or RNP directly converts

pathogenic HBBS into a non-pathogenic allele with no requirement for exogenous DNA.


<!-- Page 47 -->


32

We examined potential undesired consequences of base editing HSPCs. Base editors

can cause bystander editing of nearby nucleotides. In this study, we observed minimal (less

than 2%) non-synonymous bystander edits as a result of careful positioning of the bespoke ABE

at a CACC PAM60 (Figure 2.1a). Spurious editing of RNA can occur52 but is short-lived when

base editor mRNA or RNP is used, and did not appear to affect repopulation, viability, or

differentiation of HSCs. Off-target base editing can also occur52, although on-target and off-

target base editing in the same cell result in multiple point mutations that are less likely to be

genotoxic than multiple DSBs from on- and off-target nuclease activity52. Of the 54 identified

sites with observed off-target ABE8e-NRCH base editing in an extensive analysis of 697

computationally and experimentally nominated sites, we found no missense mutations or other

off-target edits of anticipated consequence. Nevertheless, the safety and therapeutic potential of

this approach might be further improved by testing alternative deaminase and Cas9 variants

that have been shown to minimize Cas-dependent and Cas-independent off-target base editing,

optimizing the dosage of the editing agent, or optimizing delivery methods55,68,81,84,139,140.

Although HBBG is a naturally occurring benign variant, further studies are required to better

understand the effects of this allele in combination with HBBS.

The ex vivo delivery procedure used here resembles methods currently used for HSC

editing in clinical trials118. The ABEs were electroporated as mRNA or RNP to minimize the

duration of exposure to the editing agent, which reduces off-target editing compared to DNA

delivery65. HSCs were edited using a single electroporation and transplanted into adult mice

after 24 h to minimize the duration of in vitro culture and any associated loss of multipotency.

The phenotypic rescue observed following secondary transplantation of varying proportions of

edited and unedited bone marrow establishes that the observed base editing efficiencies

substantially exceed the gene correction threshold needed for therapeutic benefit. Base-edited

patient-derived CD34+ cells thus provide a promising basis for a one-time autologous treatment

for SCD.

### 3.1 Introduction

Sickle-cell disease (SCD) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by an A•T-to-T•A

mutation in the hemoglobin subunit beta (HBB) gene, resulting in the pathogenic sickle-cell

allele (HBBS) encoding a Glu 6→Val (E6V) substitution. This mutation changes normal adult β-

globin (βA) to sickle β-globin (βS) and replacement of normal adult hemoglobin (HbA, α2β2) with

sickle hemoglobin (HbS, α2βS2).

At low oxygen tension, HbS forms rigid polymers that cause characteristic red blood cell

(RBC) shape changes and initiate a complex pathophysiology that includes hemolysis,

microvascular occlusions and inflammation. Clinical manifestations include anemia,

immunodeficiency, multi-organ damage, severe acute and chronic pain, and premature death106.

The only FDA-approved cure for SCD is allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell

transplantation. However, most patients lack ideal donors and the procedure is associated with

serious toxicities, including graft-vs-host disease and graft rejection151. Correction of the

patient’s own hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) bypasses immune complications and eliminates

the need for a tissue-compatible donor. Current strategies for therapeutic manipulation of SCD

hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) being examined in clinical trials include

lentiviral expression of an anti-sickling β-like globin152 and the use of genome editing nucleases

or base editors to activate γ-globin gene transcription for induction of fetal hemoglobin (HbF,

α2γ2)20,21,113,117,118,153 . A clinical trial using Cas9 nuclease-initiated homology-directed repair

(HDR) and an adeno-associated virus type 6 (AAV6)-delivered DNA template to correct the

SCD mutation26 was stopped due to a patient developing transfusion-dependent

pancytopenia35. Another HDR-based strategy that uses non-viral delivery of a single-stranded

oligodeoxynucleotide donor33 has been approved for a clinical trial. We recently reported a base

editing strategy using an adenine base editor to convert the pathogenic HBBS allele into the

non-pathogenic, naturally occurring Makassar allele (HBBG)19. While each of these strategies

has distinct advantages and disadvantages, reverting the SCD E6V substitution, which requires


<!-- Page 66 -->


51

a T•A-to-A•T transversion, represents the most physiological approach for disease correction.

However, base editors cannot convert T•A to A•T, and nuclease-mediated HbF induction or

HDR-mediated correction of HBB requires double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs) that cause

uncontrolled mixtures of on-target loss-of-function insertion and deletion (indel) mutations27,33,

p53 activation and chromosomal abnormalities38,40–43,154,155. Moreover, strategies that require co-

delivery of the HDR template by AAV transduction26,122 have the potential to impair HSC

engraftment27,34, which can result in transfusion-dependent pancytopenia35.

An ideal treatment for SCD would permanently revert HBBS to the wild-type allele (HBBA)

with few deleterious genomic alterations or cell state changes. Because prime editing replaces a

target segment of DNA with a specified new sequence up to hundreds of base pairs in length, it

enables the installation of targeted insertions, deletions and any base-to-base substitutions

directly into the genome of living cells and animals without requiring DSBs3,86,89,156–160. Here we

report the development of a prime editing strategy that reverts the SCD allele back to wild-type

HBBA with high on-target efficiency, low frequencies of indel by-products and minimal off-target

editing. Edited SCD patient HSPCs maintained prime editing levels at 17 weeks after

transplantation in mice, with an average of 42% of engrafted human erythroblasts and

reticulocytes across four patient donors containing at least one wild-type HBBA allele, indicating

robust editing of hematopoietic stem cells at levels that exceed the estimated therapeutic

threshold. Treated cells also showed a significant reduction in sickling when cultured in hypoxic

conditions. Minimal off-target editing was detected following the analysis of over 100

experimentally identified CIRCLE-seq-nominated candidate off-target sites engaged by the

prime editing system, suggesting a high degree of target DNA specificity. Taken together, our

results establish an early example of therapeutic prime editing in human HSCs and demonstrate

a potential strategy for a one-time autologous SCD treatment that directly corrects the sickle

globin allele back to wild-type HBB without requiring DSBs or donor DNA templates.

### 3.2 Results

3.2.1 Optimizing prime editing systems for HSPCs

We previously reported the use of prime editing to correct HBBS by plasmid transfection

in HEK293T cells containing the SCD mutation, reaching up to 58% efficiency (Figure 3.1a)3. In

contrast to HEK293T cells, HSPCs are difficult to transfect with plasmid DNA but are amenable

to RNA electroporation, an ex vivo delivery method that has been used in the clinic to

manipulate HSPCs before transplantation118,153,161. We sought to identify an RNA

electroporation-based prime editing strategy for HSPCs that incorporates recent prime editing

advances (Figures 3.1-3.3). We recently designed improved engineered pegRNAs

(epegRNAs)89 that incorporate a 3′ structured motif to protect the reverse transcriptase template

(RTT) from exonuclease degradation and an 8 nt linker that hinders potential interference

between the motif and the RTT. The linker can be designed optimally with an algorithm (pegLIT)

or less effectively by visual inspection89. In addition, we developed PEmax, an improved prime

editor (PE) architecture with optimized Cas9 and nuclear localization sequences, and codon

usage86 (Figure 3.1b). We compared editing outcomes following the electroporation of in vitro-

transcribed PE and PEmax messenger RNA (mRNA) with synthetic epegRNAs in healthy

human donor HSPCs to install various edits across four genomic loci—DNMT1 (both with a fully

optimized linker as in Figure 3.1c and with a linker chosen by inspection as in Figure 3.1d,e),

HEK293T genomic site 3 (hereafter referred to as HEK3), RUNX1 and RNF2 (Figure 3.1c). Both

PE and PEmax mRNA together with epegRNAs and nicking single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs)

supported substantial prime editing efficiencies in HSPCs (up to 85%), with PEmax conferring

1.3- to 3.5-fold average increases in editing efficiency over PE (Figure 3.1c). Thus, PEmax

mRNA can be electroporated together with synthetic epegRNAs and nicking sgRNAs to robustly

edit primary human HSPCs.

In addition to the improved PEmax architecture, our group previously reported that prime

editing outcomes can be improved by inhibiting mismatch repair (MMR) using transient co-


<!-- Page 68 -->


53

expression of MMR protein MLH1 (MLH1dn), a dominant negative MLH1 variant86, or by

installing benign or silent mutations near the desired edit that cause the prime editing

intermediate to naturally evade MMR. PE4 and PE5 systems transiently co-express MLH1dn

with PE2 and PE3, respectively86 (Figure 3.1b). Impeding MMR increases prime editing

efficiencies for small substitutions, insertions and deletions and decreases the formation of indel

by-products in a wide variety of cells86,87. To determine whether PE4max or PE5max might

increase desired editing outcomes over PE2max and PE3max in primary human HSPCs, we

electroporated in vitro-transcribed RNA encoding all prime editing components and MLH1dn into

healthy donor cells. Surprisingly, transient MLH1 expression did not improve prime editing over

PE2max or PE3max in HSPCs (Figure 3.1d,e). The +5 G > T edit at DNMT1 and the +5 G > A

edit at HBB are silent protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) alterations that may help the prime

editing intermediate natively evade MMR, without MLH1dn. However, the intermediate

mismatch to install the +1 HEK3 T > A is a known substrate for MMR86, and the prime editing

efficiency in HSPCs of +1 HEK3 T > A also does not benefit from the addition of MLH1dn.

Similarly, editing efficiencies for the +1–15 deletion at RNF2 in primary human HSPCs also did

not benefit from the addition of MLH1dn (Figure 3.1d,e).

We also compared prime editing at HBB with PE3 versus PE5 (not ‘max’ architecture)

using a pegRNA or an epegRNA in healthy human HSPCs under conditions in which prime

editing was limiting and thus the benefits of MMR evasion would be most easily manifested. We

observed no improvement in prime editing from MLH1dn expression (Figure 3.1f). Consistent

with these results, we also pretreated primary human HSPCs with small interfering RNAs

(siRNAs) targeting MLH1 and observed no benefit to PE3 prime editing outcomes at HBB

compared with the identical treatment using non-targeting siRNAs (Figure 3.1f). These

observations collectively suggest that cellular MMR may not limit the efficiency of this prime edit

in HSPCs under these conditions. A recent study reports that constitutive expression of MLH1dn

in a PE5max strategy shows increased editing efficiency compared with PE3max in human


<!-- Page 69 -->

HSPCs edited with helper-dependent adenovirus vector162. Since expression from mRNA is

much more transient than viral expression, we speculate that the timing of MLH1dn following

mRNA electroporation in HSPCs may be less effective at enhancing prime editing outcomes

than longer-lasting MLH1dn expression, or that the combination of the target edit and the

adjacent silent PAM edit is sufficient to cause the prime editing intermediate to evade MMR. We

therefore continued optimizations using electroporation-based prime editing systems with

epegRNAs and PE3max and without MLH1dn.

3.2.7 Genome-wide off-target editing analysis

Studies from multiple groups have reported that prime editing causes substantially lower

levels of off-target editing compared with other CRISPR gene editing methods, consistent with

the mechanism of prime editing, which requires three separate base pairing events between a

target DNA strand and either the pegRNA or the pegRNA-derived flap, each of which provides

an opportunity to reject an off-target sequence without modification3,97–105,157. We assessed off-

target prime editing outcomes from our HBBS correction strategy in CD34+ cells. We used the

experimental genome-wide off-target identification method CIRCLE-seq129 to nominate potential

off-target loci engaged by the Cas9 domain and guide RNAs used in the prime editing

experiments above, then measured off-target editing by HTS of the nominated sites in prime-

edited HSPCs from SCD patient donors. Since Cas9 nuclease activity when complexed with

epegRNAs is modestly decreased compared with Cas9 with the corresponding sgRNA89, we

performed CIRCLE-seq using the optimized epegRNA, using an sgRNA surrogate containing

the identical protospacer, or using the NG1 nicking sgRNA.

CIRCLE-seq nominated 515 off-target sites when using the epegRNA, 437 sites when

using an sgRNA with the epegRNA spacer and 281 sites when using the nicking sgRNA.

78 loci nominated when using the epegRNA but not when using the surrogate sgRNA are

(rhAmpSeq) to perform multiplex-targeted DNA sequencing of the top 50 sites for each of these

three categories, excluding the on-target sites and sites not amenable to pooling with the other

loci. Only 13 of the top 50 sites nominated using the surrogate sgRNA version of the epegRNA

were not also nominated in the top 50 sites using the epegRNA. All 13 were within the top 173

sites for the epegRNA. In total, from the epegRNA and surrogate sgRNA CIRCLE-seq results,

### 3.3 Discussion

Advancements in genome editing technologies have provided many options for treating

SCD. While the best strategy has not yet been determined and multiple strategies may offer

clinical benefit, reverting the SCD allele back to wild type is the most physiological approach.

Correction strategies using nuclease-initiated HDR face several challenges including donor

DNA template delivery, perturbation of engraftment potential27,34 and low ratios of desired

editing to indel by-products27,33. We describe a prime editing strategy that directly corrects the

SCD allele to wild-type HBBA without requiring double-strand DNA breaks, viral transduction or

any donor DNA templates. Following extensive optimization of key parameters including the

choice of PE3max, the design of the pegRNA, the total volume of RNAs electroporated and the

position of the nicking guide, our strategy yields up to 41% prime editing in SCD patient HSPCs

by day 3, which was maintained in bone-marrow-repopulating HSCs in transplanted mice after

17 weeks. RBCs derived from repopulated HSCs after prime editing and transplantation in mice

showed a reduction in HbS and sickling, and a rise in HbA proportional to on-target editing.

Ratios of HBBS reversion to indels were high, and off-target editing was minimal after

investigating 112 CIRCLE-seq-nominated candidate off-target sites.

There are several autologous transplantation approaches being developed or in clinical

trials towards a treatment for SCD19,26,113,117,118,122,152, and it is not yet known which strategy will

be the safest and most effective for patients. The prime editing strategy developed in this work

offers several potential advantages. It directly eliminates the pathogenic HBBS allele and

converts it back to the wild-type allele, in contrast with strategies that rely on lentiviral

expression of non-sickling globin or induction of HbF.

Current strategies to correct HBBS in SCD patient HSCs include nuclease-initiated HDR

electroporated with wild-type or a high-fidelity Cas9 nuclease complexed with a chemically

modified sgRNA and a donor DNA template either delivered as single-stranded

oligodeoxynucleotide donor33 or through recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 6


<!-- Page 89 -->


74

(rAAV6)-mediated delivery27. Compared to non-viral donor template delivery33, the prime editing

strategy developed in this study leads to similar levels of desired correction in patient HSCs with

a much higher desired edit-to-indel ratio and far fewer off-target indels. Similarly, compared with

an HDR strategy that uses rAAV6-mediated donor template delivery27, the prime editing strategy

described here results in a higher desired edit-to-indel ratio and more efficient targeting of long-

term HSCs with similar levels of pre-transplantation and post-transplantation HBBS-to- HBBA

correction. Our untreated control patient HSCs engrafted at the same level as prime-edited

patient HSCs. In contrast, HSCs with rAAV6-delivered donor template engrafted significantly

less efficiently than mock-electroporated cells27, consistent with a recent report that long-term

HSCs engraft more poorly following HDR editing with rAAV6-delivered donor templates34. These

observations suggest that prime-edited HSCs engraft at higher rates, although a well-controlled

study is needed to account for any confounding variables.

Another important advantage of the prime editing strategy described here is that it does

not require DSBs, although low frequencies of DSBs from staggered nicks can occur. These

DSB frequencies can be virtually eliminated with a PE3b strategy that prevents simultaneous

nicking of opposite DNA strands. Compared with nuclease-dependent approaches, prime

editing greatly reduces the likelihood of undesired DSB outcomes such as uncontrolled and

uncharacterized mixtures of indels, which in HBB can lead to β-thalassemia-like loss-of-

function27,33. The upper limit of tolerable indel by-products at HBB in the context of SCD gene

correction is unknown. However, HDR-based approaches with high levels of indels may cause a

β-thalassemia-like pathophysiology in erythroid precursors, with deficiency of β-globin protein,

accumulation of toxic free α-globin, maturation arrest and apoptosis33,167,168. A high edit-to-indel

ratio as achieved with editing methods that do not require DSBs maximizes the number of

precisely corrected cells administered to patients. In comparison with nuclease-dependent

approaches, prime editing also reduces the likelihood of large deletions, chromosomal loss,

translocations, chromothripsis and other undesired cell state changes38,40–43. Several studies


<!-- Page 90 -->


75

have used whole-genome sequencing, whole-transcriptome sequencing and other broad

analytical methods following prime editing to assess potential genome- or transcriptome-wide

changes in mammalian cells and, thus far, neither changes in single-nucleotide variants, indels,

telomere length, endogenous retrotransposon activity, gene expression or splicing nor any off-

target RNA editing have been reported100,101,103–105.

An additional feature of the prime editing strategy studied here is that it does not require

DNA delivery, viral transduction or drug selection to enrich edited cells. DNA delivery is required

for HDR and gene therapy, but can also lead to increased toxicity, lower engraftment frequency

or insertional mutagenesis27,34,114,137,138,155.

We compared CIRCLE-seq off-target site nomination using an sgRNA containing the

epegRNA spacer sequence to CIRCLE-seq using the epegRNA directly. The overlap between

### 4.1 Introduction

CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD) is an X-linked, neurological disorder caused by

pathogenic mutations in the cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) gene173. CDKL5 is a

serine/threonine kinase with key roles in brain development and function174 including dendritic

microtubule regulation175 and maintenance of dendritic spine morphology176,177. Though

originally thought of as an early-onset form of Rett syndrome178, CDD is now considered a

distinct disorder179,180 with hundreds of causative mutations in the CDKL5 gene identified in

patients178,181–191. While most mutations that cause the disorder are spontaneous de novo

mutations, at least one case of a maternally-inherited pathogenic variant of CDKL5 has been

described192. Pathogenic mutations in CDD typically result in haploinsufficiency either through

full or partial loss of CDKL5 catalytic activity193,194, though at least one example of a

hypermorphic mutation has been described195, and some lesser-studied CDD mutations may

behave similarly to dominant negative mutations found via functional and biochemical

assays176,196,197.

Symptoms of CDD begin in early postnatal life, correlating with peak CDKL5

expression173,176,196. A major clinical manifestation of CDD is infantile-onset seizures which are

treatment-resistant, however patients also experience developmental delay, intellectual

disability, extreme difficulty sleeping, visual impairment, gastrointestinal issues, and respiratory

difficulties among other symptoms173,194. As of this writing, treatment for CDD is limited to

symptom management. Symptom management options include broad-range anti-seizure

medications (ASMs) like levetiracetam, the only FDA-approved ASM specifically for CDD called

ganaxolone, ketogenic diet, and non-FDA approved cannabidiol derivatives198,199. Currently,

there are no curative therapies available for CDD, though investigational disease-modifying

therapeutics have been pursued with varying effectiveness198,199. Current investigational

therapeutic strategies include epigenetic reactivation of CDKL5 expression200 and a gene

therapy to deliver a functional copy of the CDKL5 protein to the brain201. Though each of these


<!-- Page 100 -->


85

strategies have unique advantages, none of them directly address the underlying genetic

mutations that cause CDD. In contrast, development of a genome editing therapeutic has the

potential to be curative by directly correcting pathogenic CDKL5 mutations.

Because CDD mutations can be caused by a suite of genetic changes such as deletions,

duplications, transition or transversion mutations178,181–191,195, development of a genome editing

strategy for CDD must utilize a genome editing tool capable of performing precise changes of

any variation. Traditional CRISPR nuclease-mediated genome editing results in uncontrolled

mixtures of insertion and deletion (indel) alleles5,10, a strategy best suited for disruption of a

locus, but not the correction of specific insertions, deletions, or other small mutations that cause

CDD. Additionally, nuclease-based strategies require double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs) which

can result in p53 activation41,43 and undesirable chromosomal abnormalities like large deletions

or chromothripsis37,42,202. In contrast, prime editing can encode deletions, insertions, point

mutations, and any combination thereof across hundreds of base pairs at a targeted locus in

living cells without requiring a DSB intermediate3,86,89,157–160, making it an optimal choice for the

development of corrective genome editing strategies for CDD. In this work, we focus on three

uniquely prime editable (i.e. difficult or impossible to correct precisely with base editing53,54 or

Cas9 nuclease editing) pathogenic mutations in CDKL5, namely a single nucleotide deletion

(c.1412delA), a splice acceptor variant surrounded by additional adenines (c.826-1 G > A), and

the installation of clustering pathogenic mutations in the eighth exon of CDKL5181. Our studies

demonstrate that prime editing can efficiently correct multiple classes of pathogenic CDKL5

variants.

We report the development of prime editing strategies for all three regions of interest

with high on-target efficiency and with minimal indel by-products. We were able to specifically

target the pathogenic allele harboring the equivalent c.1412delA mutation in murine Cdkl5 with

correction efficiencies up to 40% by utilizing a bespoke prime editor comprised of a SpCas9-

NRCH DNA targeting domain60 and PE6 variants (PE6b-d) with evolved and/or engineered


<!-- Page 101 -->

reverse transcriptase (RT) domains88. We optimized a previously reported c.1412delA

correction strategy86 and achieved 42.3% and 36.2% desired correction with high specificity in

patient primary fibroblasts using PE3max and PE6c88 respectively. Finally, we demonstrate the

applicability of prime editing to various other pathogenic mutations in CDKL5, including

correction of c.826-1 G > A at an average of 8.8% and installing a series of seven pathogenic

mutations or seed edits for pathogenic mutations in exon 8, a known hotspot for CDKL5

mutations181, at nearly 30% efficiency. Taken together, our results show that prime editing

systems enable the efficient and precise correction of multiple types of pathogenic CDKL5

mutations, even simultaneously with a single prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA), and without

requiring DSBs.

### 4.2 Results

4.2.1 Optimizing prime editing to correct c.1412delA in murine Cdkl5

Nuclease-based editing strategies for the correction of specific nucleotides could result

in more indel alleles than alleles with the desired correction26,30–32. This editing strategy is of

limited therapeutic benefit for c.1412delA as it is located in the catalytic domain where both in-

frame and out-of-frame mutations can manifest in disease199. Indel alleles created by nuclease

editing are predictable but uncontrollable18, making it hard to specify a particular indel allele as

the desired outcome. Though base editors are more precise and cause fewer indel alleles than

nuclease-mediated editing strategies, deletions like c.1412delA are not addressable with base

editing technology. Base editors enable efficient A•T-to-G•C editing54 or C•G-to-T•A53 editing

and vice versa, but base editors cannot revert a deletion mutation. Thus, c.1412delA represents

a uniquely prime-editable pathogenic variant of CDKL5. Our group previously optimized a

pegRNA to correct c.1412delA via electroporation of in vitro transcribed PE mRNA and synthetic

pegRNA into patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)86. We sought to further


<!-- Page 102 -->


87

improve this editing strategy with the use of engineered pegRNAs89 and a suite of newly

evolved and engineered PE6s88 at both mouse and human CDKL5.

Because the mouse model for the c.1412delA mutation is not humanized, we first

developed a prime editing strategy to correct the equivalent c.1412delA mutation in the murine

Cdkl5 gene to enable future in vivo studies. The c.1412delA mutation occurred in a female

patient, so the patient still has one healthy CDKL5 gene intact. Consequently, we reasoned that

an optimal genome editing strategy would preferentially target the disease allele while

bypassing the healthy allele. To this end, we developed an allele-specific prime editing strategy

that incorporates recent prime editing advances. We designed and screened engineered

pegRNAs (epegRNAs) that include a structured 3’ motif which protects the reverse transcriptase

template (RTT) from endogenous exonuclease degradation89. We included a dominant negative

version of MLH1 (MLH1dn) to downregulate mismatch repair (MMR) as inhibition of MMR leads

to improved prime editing outcomes86,87. We also utilized PE6 variants88, or next-generation

prime editors with evolved and/or rationally designed mutations in the Cas9 or reverse

transcriptase domains. In order to specifically target the disease allele, we used the SpCas9-

which recognize NRCH protospacer adjacent motifs (PAMs), where N is any nucleotide, R is

adenine or guanine, and H is any nucleotide except guanine. The pathogenic c.1412delA

mutation allows the creation of an NRCH PAM (TGCA), and correction of the mutation disrupts

the NRCH PAM (TGTCA) (Figure 4.1a).

4.2.4 Genome-wide off-target editing analysis in patient primary fibroblasts

After optimizing the prime editing strategy for corrective editing of c.1412delA in CDKL5

and quantifying its efficacy in patient primary fibroblasts, we next sought to quantify any off-

target editing. Prime editing has widely been reported to have substantially lower levels of off-

target editing compared to other CRISPR-based gene editing methods79,97–105, reflecting the

multiple steps at which an off-target sequence can be rejected without modification3. To assess

off-target prime editing outcomes from our PEmax and PE6c correction strategies in patient

primary fibroblasts, we used Cas-OFFinder, a computational method for nominating potential

off-target loci128. We used the Cas-OFFinder algorithm to nominate off-target loci with up to

three mismatches to the target protospacer sequences of the epegRNA and the nicking sgRNA.

For the epegRNA, 15 off-target loci were nominated (Peg OT1-15). Just 3 off-target loci were

exactly 3 mismatches.

We used HTS to quantify off-target editing at each of the nominated loci. For the

epegRNA off-targets, we quantified the mutation frequency at the position of the first substitution

that would be encoded by the epegRNA RTT as this position is the most likely nucleotide to be

changed during prime editing3,79. Since the probability of an incorrect base call for our HTS

method is 1 in 1000 bases204, we established a threshold of 0.1% in our analysis for bona fide

epegRNA-dependent off-target substitution. Though our preliminary analysis is not yet powered

enough to perform tests for statistical significance, we observed that epegRNA-dependent off-

target substitutions in PE3max-treated or PE6c-treated fibroblasts were largely similar to that of

untreated fibroblasts (Figure 4.4a).  Only at Peg OT9 did we observe any editing above the

with previous reports that prime editing leads to minimal pegRNA-dependent off-target

4.2.5 Corrective prime editing of alternative pathogenic CDKL5 mutations

There are hundreds of pathogenetic mutations known to cause CDD178,181–192. Because

of this, we sought to apply prime editing strategies to other loci of interest in CDKL5. One locus

of interest is a pathogenic mutation at a splice site acceptor, c.826-1 G > A. This CDKL5 variant

is uniquely prime-editable given the short-comings of nuclease-based editing and the presence

of multiple other adenines in the editing window that could result in bystander A > G editing if

the locus were targeted by a base editor.

In order to begin initial optimizations for a corrective c.826-1 G > A prime editing

strategy, we first created two heterozygous HEK293T cell lines harboring the pathogenic

mutation about 30% of alleles. After establishing the cell lines, we then designed and screened

epegRNAs that encode the desired corrective edit (+24 A > G) and multiple silent mutations

near the desired corrective edit (+17-21 TTTAC > CCTGT) (Figure 4.5a). These benign

mutations help the prime editing intermediate to naturally evade MMR, a DNA repair process

known to decrease desired prime editing outcomes86,87. We conducted an epegRNA screen by

transfecting PEmax-∆RNaseH, MHL1dn, and various epegRNAs into our model cell lines

(Figure 4.5b). While editing efficiencies were low, we observed several epegRNAs with desired

editing percentages above 0.7% across all alleles. We elected to use the epegRNA with PBS

and RTT lengths of 11 and 33 nt respectively reaching an average of 0.75 ± 0.32% editing for

additional optimization.

Next, we wanted to determine the most optimal prime editor for our corrective strategy

(Figure 4.5c). We also screened for the most optimal nicking sgRNA position with 3 nicking

sgRNAs in total (NG1, NG2, NG3, Figure 4.5c). NG3 was designed for edit-specific

complementary nicking in which nicking does not occur until after the desired edit has been

installed. This edit-specific nicking sgRNA design leads to minimal indel formation3. Unlike NG1

and NG2, NG3 utilizes an NGA PAM instead of the canonical NGG PAM because SpCas9 can

have residual catalytic activity on NGA PAMs44,205. We observed that PE6c resulted in the

highest correction efficiency with up to 9.8% desired editing when paired with NG2 (Figure

continued optimizations lead to increased desired editing and potentially increased indel

composition of matter and a single clinical trial for a group of patients as opposed to the

development of multiple compositions of matter for each individual patient, and consequently

multiple clinical trials. Thus, we chose exon 8 as a model site for demonstrating the ability of a

single epegRNA to modify multiple bases in a region like the catalytic domain where multiple

pathogenic mutations cluster. As a proof-of-principle, we designed two epegRNA to install five

endogenous exonucleases before resolution of editing via DNA repair. Having a longer RTT that

The lack of approved disease-modifying therapeutics for CDD highlights the urgent

unmet medical need of CDD patients and their caregivers. While a gene therapy that would

deliver a functional copy of CDKL5 is being developed, this therapeutic strategy may be

intractable for patients with dominant negative mutations206. Additionally, the dosage sensitivity

of many genetic epilepsy disorders, including CDD where overexpression of CDKL5 has been

reported to manifest in disease207, limits the applicability of a gene replacement therapy since

endogenous transcriptional control of the target gene would be lost206,208. The most

physiological approach to treating CDD would be to revert the disease alleles back to wildtype.

We developed PEmax-NRCH and PE6-NRCH strategies capable of enabling 38% allele-

specific correction of c.1412delA in heterozygous murine N2a cells. Though development of a


<!-- Page 119 -->


104

PE-NRCH correction strategy in human CDKL5 was not initially successful without the addition

of a non-silent seed edit, we demonstrated nearly 40% correction of the c.1412delA allele in

patient primary fibroblasts with PE6c and a previously reported pegRNA converted to an

epegRNA. Future studies utilizing our optimized non-linker epegRNA may result in even higher

levels of correction. Initial off-target editing analyses with Cas-OFFinder-nominated loci revealed

that our prime editing strategy was highly-specific. Additional analyses with more replicates and

at sites that are experimentally nominated will help us develop a more comprehensive

understanding of off-target editing for our c.1412delA corrective prime editing strategies. Initial

experiments for the correction of c.826-1 G > A resulted in up to 9.8% prime editing with PE6c,

and prime editing at a mutational hotspot in exon 8 resulted in 25.4% installation of seven

additional CDKL5 mutations or relevant seed edits. Our results demonstrate that the

development of prime editing strategies, including those with the recently described PE6

variants, lead to robust levels of editing across the CDKL5 gene.

One pertinent question that remains for the development of a genome editing strategy

for CDD is the level of correction needed for therapeutic benefit. While it is currently unknown

how much gene correction would be necessary for a potentially curative CDD therapeutic, other

rare diseases, including the related Rett syndrome, have established therapeutic thresholds

from 5-20% correction164,165,209–213. Many of our genome editing strategies for pathogenic CDKL5

variants meet or exceed 20% corrective editing in various model systems. Given the level of

corrective editing we are able to achieve in our current models, we are encouraged that we may

meet or exceed the therapeutic threshold. In order to better characterize the therapeutic benefit

of our genome editing strategies, we must test them in vitro in patient-derived iPSCs

differentiated toward neurons and cortical organoids, and in vivo in a relevant mouse model to

assess rescue of protein expression, phosphorylation of downstream CDKL5 targets,

biochemical and behavioral deficits associated with CDD in these models. Through these


<!-- Page 120 -->


105

upcoming studies, we may be able to better understand what level of corrective genome editing

is necessary to be disease-modifying for CDD.

Another important question in the development of CDD therapeutics is timing of drug

administration. Since CDD is early-onset and clinical symptoms occur within the first few months

of life, there have historically been concerns about the therapeutic window at which a patient

must be treated208. A recent study has shown that restoration of CDKL5 expression in adult

mice rescued CDD-associated phenotypes177. These findings suggest that the ability to treat

CDD beyond early infancy may be possible, another encouraging sign to pursue the

development of a genome editing treatment for CDD patients.

The use of prime editing to correct pathogenic mutations at therapeutically relevant

levels in model systems has been successful for diseases in which all or some of the patients

share one mutation, as is the case with sickle cell disease79. Thus, one might consider prime

editing of limited use for a disease like CDD in which mutations are spontaneous and occur

throughout the gene. Though we focus on two particular pathogenic mutations, the optimization

of corrective editing for these mutations could benefit other patients with nearby known

pathogenic mutations. For example, our optimized prime editing strategy for c.1412delA could

also be used to correct c.1417dup (rs786204970) and c.1419del (rs2147160726). There are two

other known pathogenic mutations at or near c.826-1 G > A, namely c.826-1 G > C

(rs587783149) and c.826-2 A > G (rs1060501859). These other two pathogenic mutations could

also be benefited by a fully optimized corrective prime editing strategy designed for c.826-1 G >

A. Additionally, we demonstrate efficient insertion of pathogenic mutations in exon 8 over

multiple amino acids as proof of concept that a single epegRNA could modify a locus where

many pathogenic mutations have been found. Since a single epegRNA could modify up to 80

bases with high efficiency3, future studies could theoretically optimize the correction of up to 80

pathogenic alleles that cluster in the catalytic domain of CDKL5. Furthermore, prime editing

technologies have been developed that can modify exon-sized fragments of DNA. Twin prime


<!-- Page 121 -->


106

editing (twinPE) uses two epegRNAs to synthesize complementary strands of DNA, enabling

modifications of DNA up to 780 base pairs158. Combined with serine recombinases, twinPE

could enable DNA modifications up to 37kb158. Given the high frequency of pathogenic

missense mutations in the catalytic domain of CDKL5, correction of CDD mutations would be an

excellent future therapeutic application for these precise, large-scale genome editing strategies.

A final consideration as we apply our CDKL5 genome editing strategy to increasingly

complex models would be the delivery modality. Adeno-associated virus (AAV), particularly

adeno-associated virus type 9 (AAV9), remains a common delivery modality with gene therapies

for rare neurological disorders that are FDA-approved or in clinical development69,90,201. Prime

editors and their necessary components for editing have typically exceed the 4.7kb packaging

limit of AAV70,71, but efficient prime editing, even in vivo in the mouse central nervous system,

with dual AAVs has been described with PEmax-∆RNaseH and PE6d88,91. In addition to AAV

delivery, we may consider the use of non-viral delivery agents such as engineered virus-like

particles which have recently shown efficacy with the prime editor214.

In summary, prime editors represent a uniquely-suited precision genome editing tool for

the correction of pathogenic mutations in CDKL5. Corrective prime editing strategies described

in this study are efficient, even in primary patient cells, and could lay the groundwork for the

development of a disease-modifying genome editing treatment for CDD patients.

## Chapter 5 : Conclusion

Precision genome editors, namely base and prime editors, do not require DSB formation

or donor DNA template delivery. Consequently, they are powerful tools for the development of

potentially curative therapeutics by avoiding excessive unwanted indel allele formation and

nuclease-associated genotoxicities. In this dissertation, I describe the comprehensive

development of base and prime editing strategies for sickle cell disease and for CDKL5

deficiency disorder. The disclosed strategies use state-of-the-art evolved and engineered

components, in addition to bespoke editors created particularly for the loci of interest.

Ex vivo electroporation is an established method for the therapeutic modification of

sickle cell patient HSPCs. We developed a base editing strategy to convert the sickle cell allele

to a naturally-occurring and non-pathogenic allele (Makassar) with ex vivo electroporation of

ABE8e-NRCH mRNA. With our base editing strategy, we were able to demonstrate therapeutic

levels of HBBS conversion to HBBG. We also demonstrated a reduction in sickle cell pathology

in treated reticulocytes and in various other parameters like spleen size in a sickle cell mouse

model. One limitation of our base editing strategy was the presence of off-target base editing at

54 computationally- or experimentally-nominated cites. Though no off-target loci are anticipated

to be of any clinical significance, future studies for our base editing strategy could consider the

integration of mutations, like V106W in Cas9, which have previously been shown to reduce off-

target editing with ABE8e.

Our ex vivo prime editing strategy for sickle cell disease, which has the advantage of

directly reverting the sickle cell allele back to wildtype (HBBA), also exceeded the anticipated

20% correction needed for therapeutic benefit in patients. PE reversion of HBBS-to-HBBA led to

a significant reduction in sickle cell phenotypes like hypoxic sickling in treated reticulocytes.

Additionally, off-target formation was minimal, with the nicking sgRNA producing the only bona

fide off-target. Our ddPCR analysis suggests that switching the nicking sgRNA to one specific


<!-- Page 128 -->


113

for the edited strand would eliminate the only detectable off-target editing. Important future

studies for this project include screening PE6 variants to determine if any of the evolved and/or

engineered PE6 variants, when used in our 2x electroporation protocol, can significantly

improve editing outcomes compared to PE3max, in addition to scaling up our editing protocol to

edit millions of HSPCs at once.

When considering the most optimal genome editing tool for sickle cell disease, the

benefits of precision genome editing tools are clear. Both base and prime editing lead to much

higher desired edit-to-indel ratios than any nuclease-mediated genome editing strategy. This

highly increased desired edit-to-indel ratio is a direct consequence of base and prime editors not

requiring DSB formation. Additionally, neither strategy requires the delivery of a donor DNA

template which has previously led to impaired HSC engraftment and poor clinical outcomes

when the template is delivered via AAV6. Both precision genome editing strategies have a

unique advantage—base editing leads to higher HBBS conversion than prime editing thus far.

However, prime editing has the advantage of being the most physiologically-relevant precision

genome editing tool for sickle cell disease through direct reversion of HBBS to HBBA with

minimal off-target formation. The value of our precision genome editing studies is that both

detail clinically viable methods of treating sickle cell disease. Carefully controlled head-to-head

studies will be required to determine which precision genome editor leads to better clinical

outcomes. It would be ideal if these studies also consider the addition of variants that could

potentially improve outcomes for either editor, such as incorporation of V106W for ABE8e-

NRCH or use of PE6 in our 2xPE3max system.

In addition to therapeutic editing for sickle cell disease, in this dissertation I describe the

development of prime editing strategies for 3 loci of interest in CDKL5 using evolved, size-

minimized prime editors compatible with in vivo CNS delivery. For the c.1412delA variant, we

developed a bespoke, allele-specific correction strategy for murine Cdkl5 with PEmax-NRCH,

PE6b-NRCH, and PE6c-NRCH each reaching an average of 38% corrective editing. We


<!-- Page 129 -->


114

improved a previously described PEmax editing strategy for c.1412delA in human CDKL5,

leading to 33% correction in a homozygous HEK293T cell line with PE6c and over 40%

correction in primary patient fibroblasts with PE3max. Finally, we achieved 9% corrective editing

for another locus, c.826-1 G > A, and we provided proof-of-principle evidence that a single

epegRNA could theoretically correct seven pathogenic variants that cluster in exon 8 at over

25% editing efficiency.

The significance of our work, especially in the context of current therapeutic options for

CDD patients, is that there are currently no other reported precision genome editing

therapeutics in development for CDD. In fact, the most similar therapeutic in development is a

gene therapy which does not correct pathogenic mutations, and that has many outstanding

questions such as the physiological implications of expressing CDKL5 without endogenous

transcriptional control and the utility of such a drug for patients with hypermorphic mutations.

Though only one such patient has been described, it is not unreasonable to think there are

others given the hundreds of pathogenic CDKL5 mutations and the lack of knowledge

surrounding the vast majority of them.

Important future studies for our CDKL5 genome editing strategies will be to quantify

editing and rescue of pathogenic phenotypes in additional in vitro models such as neurons and

cortical organoids differentiated from patient-derived iPSCs, and in vivo with appropriate mouse

models. In vivo editing will require the use of AAVs. Use of size-minimized PEmax-∆RNaseH

and PE6 variants will allow us to pursue a dual AAV strategy (as opposed to a triple AAV

strategy with full-length PEmax) which has previously been shown to be highly efficient in the

mouse central nervous system. Successful correction of pathogenic CDKL5 mutations in vivo

with a commonly used viral delivery method will be an important part of a preclinical package.

Additional future studies could incorporate the use of twinPE and serine recombinases to

recode large, exon-sized stretches of DNA, which would be particularly useful in the context of a

disease like CDD where pathogenic mutations stretch across the entire gene.


<!-- Page 130 -->


115

The level of editing required for therapeutic benefit for CDD is not yet known. Dose

escalation studies across advanced preclinical models could help us determine a therapeutic

threshold. Because there is evidence from other rare diseases that as little as 5-20% correction

could be potentially curative, we are hopeful that our editing strategies, most of which exceed

20% correction, will reach the therapeutic threshold.

The speed at which base editors, and soon prime editors, have entered the clinic

suggests a bright and exciting future for precision genome editing. Exceedingly quick and robust

technology development for the improvement base and prime editors has accelerated their

therapeutic application. This dissertation demonstrates the feasibility of clinically relevant base

and prime editing corrective strategies for sickle cell disease, both of which exceed the

estimated therapeutic threshold. Additionally, this work details multiple efficient corrective prime

editing strategies for several pathogenic CDKL5 mutations in preclinical models. Taken

together, the studies detailed in this dissertation mark important steps toward making precision

genome editing a therapeutic reality for sickle cell disease and CDKL5 deficiency disorder

patients.
